author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or vessel pairs

modules.moduleName: Heart Anatomy: Chambers, Valves, and Vessels
modules.description: An introduction to the structural anatomy of the human heart, focusing on identifying the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels that enter and exit the heart. Students explore a detailed 3D heart model and learn the anatomical names and locations of all key structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and name the four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
Identify and name the four valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral (bicuspid), aortic
Locate and name the major vessels: superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Display the complete heart model in the center of the workspace to establish the overall anatomy and orientation.
clips.narration: Welcome to the heart anatomy module. The human heart is a muscular four-chambered organ that pumps blood throughout the body. Let's begin by exploring the overall structure. You're looking at a three-dimensional model of the heart in anatomical position, with the anterior surface facing toward you.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the four chambers with color-coded labels and slight positional emphasis to distinguish atria from ventricles.
clips.narration: The heart is divided into four chambers: two upper chambers called atria, and two lower chambers called ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body. The right ventricle pumps that blood to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Add visual labels for the four valves positioned at their anatomical locations on the heart model.
clips.narration: Between the chambers and vessels lie four valves that ensure one-way blood flow and prevent backflow. The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries. The mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Display vessel labels positioned around the heart model to show all six major vessels and their connections.
clips.narration: Several major vessels connect to the heart. The superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood from the upper and lower body into the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Finally, the aorta exits the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the entire body.

modules.moduleName: Blood Flow Through the Heart: The Dual Circulation
modules.description: A guided trace of the complete path blood takes through the heart, moving through both the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit. Students follow animated blood droplets and highlighted pathways as the narration explains the sequence of chambers, valves, and vessels involved in one complete cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the path of deoxygenated blood from the vena cava through the right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, and pulmonary arteries
Trace the path of oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins through the left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, and aorta
Explain the sequence of events in a single cardiac cycle
Distinguish between the pulmonary circuit (right heart) and the systemic circuit (left heart)

clips.changeMeaning: Display the heart with both blood droplet markers positioned at their starting locations to represent deoxygenated and oxygenated blood simultaneously.
clips.narration: Now let's trace the complete path of blood through the heart. Blood circulation involves two circuits: the pulmonary circuit, which carries blood to and from the lungs, and the systemic circuit, which carries blood to and from the body. These circuits work simultaneously in the left and right sides of the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Animate the deoxygenated blood droplet moving from the vena cava entry point into the right atrium, and update the flow stage label.
clips.narration: Let's follow the deoxygenated blood first. It returns from the body's tissues through the superior and inferior vena cava and enters the right atrium. This blood is oxygen-poor and has a dark bluish color. Once the right atrium fills, it contracts, pushing the blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Animate the deoxygenated droplet moving through the pulmonary valve and arteries, while the oxygenated droplet enters the left atrium from the pulmonary veins.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts and forces the deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, which carry it to both lungs where it will be oxygenated. Meanwhile, oxygenated blood from the lungs returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, ready to enter the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Animate the oxygenated droplet through the mitral valve, into the left ventricle, and through the aortic valve into the aorta. Highlight the thicker left ventricular wall.
clips.narration: The oxygenated blood in the left atrium contracts and pushes the blood through the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, into the left ventricle. The left ventricle has a much thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle because it must generate enough pressure to push blood through the entire body via the aorta. When the left ventricle contracts, it forces the blood through the aortic valve and into the aorta, beginning the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Reset the blood droplets to their starting positions and show the complete heart with slight rotation to emphasize the continuous cyclical nature of blood flow.
clips.narration: This entire cycle repeats with every heartbeat. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the low-pressure pulmonary circuit to the lungs. The left side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood through the high-pressure systemic circuit to the entire body. The coordinated contractions of all four chambers, controlled by the conduction system of the heart, ensure efficient and continuous circulation.

modules.moduleName: Ventricular Wall Thickness and Pressure Demands
modules.description: An exploration of the structural relationship between ventricular wall thickness and the pressure requirements of the pulmonary versus systemic circuits. Students examine a cross-sectional view of the ventricles side by side and learn why the left ventricle's myocardium is substantially thicker than the right ventricle's.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain the relationship between wall thickness and the pressure required to perfuse the pulmonary circuit versus the systemic circuit
Compare the workload of the right ventricle (pulmonary circulation) to the left ventricle (systemic circulation)
Describe how myocardial thickness reflects the functional demands placed on each ventricle
Predict which ventricle would hypertrophy in response to chronic conditions affecting pulmonary versus systemic pressure

clips.changeMeaning: Display both ventricles side by side in cross-section, clearly showing the difference in wall thickness between right and left.
clips.narration: The left and right ventricles are not identical in structure. The most notable difference is that the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardial wall than the right ventricle. This difference is directly related to the pressure demands of the two circuits they serve. Let's examine the ventricles in cross-section to understand why.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the right ventricle with a light glow and display the pulmonary circuit pressure range. Emphasize the thin myocardial wall.
clips.narration: The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary circuit to the lungs and back. The lungs are nearby, and the pulmonary arteries and capillaries offer relatively low resistance to blood flow. As a result, the right ventricle must generate only about 15 to 25 millimeters of mercury of pressure. This modest pressure requirement is reflected in the right ventricle's thin, crescent-shaped myocardial wall.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the left ventricle with a strong glow and display the systemic circuit pressure range. Emphasize the thick myocardial wall in contrast to the right ventricle.
clips.narration: The left ventricle pumps blood through the systemic circuit to the entire body and back. The systemic circulation has much greater resistance due to the distance blood must travel and the density of tissue it must perfuse. The left ventricle must generate approximately 120 millimeters of mercury of pressure to overcome this resistance. This much higher pressure requirement is reflected in the left ventricle's substantially thicker, muscular myocardial wall.

clips.changeMeaning: Maintain side-by-side view with both ventricles highlighted, reinforcing the structural-functional relationship between wall thickness and pressure demands.
clips.narration: The relationship between wall thickness and pressure is straightforward: the higher the pressure a chamber must generate, the thicker its muscular wall must be. This follows the law of Laplace in cardiac physiology, where wall thickness is proportional to the pressure the wall must withstand. The five-fold difference in required pressures between the pulmonary and systemic circuits explains why the left ventricular wall is roughly three times thicker than the right.

clips.changeMeaning: Display both ventricles with annotations highlighting that wall thickness is an adaptation to pressure workload, reinforcing the structure-function relationship.
clips.narration: Understanding this relationship has clinical significance. Chronic hypertension causes the left ventricle to hypertrophy as it works against elevated systemic pressure. Conversely, chronic pulmonary hypertension causes the right ventricle to hypertrophy. By examining myocardial wall thickness, clinicians can infer the hemodynamic stresses a patient's heart has experienced and predict future cardiac complications.
